White precipitate with KOH indicates cation forms insoluble hydroxide (e.g., Al3+, Fe3+, Cr3+, Zn2+, Cu2+ (blue), etc.) but also many cations produce white precipitate (e.g., Ca2+, Mg2+, Ba2+, Sr2+, etc.) However some produce colored precipitates. White suggests maybe group 2 metal (Ca, Sr, Ba) or Al3+, Fe3+ (brown), etc. But we also have no flame color, so not Na, K, Ca (Ca gives orange-red flame), Ba gives green, Sr red, etc. No flame color suggests maybe a cation that doesn't give characteristic flame (most transition metals). Also sample is colorless, so no colored cation like Cu2+ (blue) or Fe3+ (yellow/brown). So likely a transition metal that is colorless in solution, e.g., Zn2+ (colorless), Mg2+ (colorless), Al3+ (colorless but acidic). But Al3+ solution often slightly acidic. Also hydroxide of Al is white gelatinous. Zn(OH)2 white. Mg(OH)2 white. So possible cations: Mg2+, Zn2+, Al3+, maybe Ca2+ (but flame color). So we have to narrow list based on these tests.

We also have chloride test positive: white AgCl precipitate indicates Cl- present. So the salt contains chloride anion. So the unknown salt is a chloride of the cation.

Thus cation possibilities: MgCl2, ZnCl2, AlCl3 (though AlCl3 is not stable in water, hydrolyzes to acidic solution). Also maybe FeCl3 (but Fe3+ solution yellow/brown). So likely Mg2+, Zn2+, Al3+.
